newsitem.title: UK: B.A.T shares extend losses on dividend.
newsitem.headline: B.A.T shares extend losses on dividend.

text.p: Shares in B.A.T Industries Plc extended their losses by mid-afternoon, dropping nearly four percent after the cigarette maker surprisingly held its dividend steady, analysts said.
By 1350 GMT, B.A.T shares were off 21p at 519p on volume of nearly 10 million, bucking the sharply higher FTSE 100 index.

"I think the two main factors were the dividend, which was a surprise to everyone, and the U.S. domestic cigarette market, which is under greater pressure than previously believed," said Simon Willis, tobacco analyst at Charterhouse Tilney.
B.A.T announced a maintained interim dividend of 10 pence per share and an unchanged final dividend of no less than last year's 16.0 pence.
Analysts had forecast an increase to between 10.7p and 10.8p per share at the half-year stage and a five to eight percent rise in the final dividend.

"The maintenance of the dividend at 1996 levels shows some ill grace on the part of B.A.T management, which traditionally has had a commitment to a progressive dividend policy," said Tim Young, an analyst at SocGen.
B.A.T assured investors that a landmark settlement of legal claims against the tobacco industry in the United States announced in June was unlikely to affect other countries.

The group announced pre-tax profits of 1.247 billion pounds in the six months to June 30, down 64 million or five percent on the first half of 1996, due mainly to the 61 million pounds impact of sterling's strength.
Analysts had forecast profits between 1.237 billion stg and 1.301 billion stg.
"Earnings weren't exactly as expected because of a higher than expected tax charge. Frankly, that doesn't change my valuation. Operating profit was exactly as expected," Young said.
Young valued B.A.T at 673-822p, taking into account all aspects of the settlement, at least 150p above current prices.
B.A.T Chief Executive Martin Broughton said he would accept no fundamental changes to the proposed settlement in the U.S. with state attorneys.

He also said there was little advantage in a "straight demerger" of the group's financial services because of "financial inefficiencies" and the company "would need to await more clarity on FIDs (foreign income dividends)."
SocGen's Willis said he was a buyer of the stock based on the upside potential of a demerger.
